def: The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of suitable frequency falls on it.
points: Electrons emitted this way are called photoelectrons.
Law 1: For a given metal, photoelectric emission starts only above a minimum frequency, called the threshold frequency.
Law 2: Photoelectric current (number of electrons emitted per second) is directly proportional to the intensity of incident light, provided frequency is above threshold.
Law 3: Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depends only on the frequency of light, not on its intensity.
Law 4: Emission is instantaneous — there is no measurable time delay even for very weak light.
These laws could not be explained by the wave theory of light, which led to Einstein's photon theory.
formula: Photoelectric current proportional to intensity I; KEmax depends only on frequency v

diagram.draw: Draw an evacuated glass tube. Inside, show a metal plate C (cathode/emitter) on the left and a collector plate A (anode) on the right. Show light rays falling on C. Connect both plates to a battery with a variable voltage and a microammeter in series to measure photoelectric current. Label 'incident light', 'photoelectrons', 'battery', 'microammeter'.

example: Sodium has threshold frequency 5 x 10^14 Hz. Light of frequency 4 x 10^14 Hz (below threshold) causes no emission however intense it is; light of 6 x 10^14 Hz causes emission even if dim.
tip: State all four laws clearly and mention that intensity affects only photocurrent, never KEmax — this distinction is commonly tested.

def: Einstein explained the photoelectric effect by treating light as a stream of photons, each of energy hv, that transfer their energy to electrons in one collision.
points: A photon of frequency v has energy E = h v, where h is Planck's constant.
When a photon strikes an electron in the metal, it is absorbed completely by one electron.
Part of this energy (work function, phi0) is used to free the electron from the metal surface.
The remaining energy appears as kinetic energy of the emitted electron.
So: h v = phi0 + KEmax, which is Einstein's photoelectric equation.
This equation explains why KEmax depends on frequency and not on intensity (more photons just means more electrons, not higher energy each).
formula: h v = phi0 + (1/2) m v_max^2 = phi0 + KEmax

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Photon of energy h v"] --> B["Hits electron in metal"]
  B --> C["Part used as work function phi0"]
  B --> D["Rest becomes KEmax of electron"]
  C --> E["h v equals phi0 plus KEmax"]
  D --> E

example: For a metal with phi0 = 2 eV, light of frequency giving hv = 3.5 eV: KEmax = 3.5 - 2 = 1.5 eV.
tip: Always write the equation hv = phi0 + KEmax first, then substitute — this is a guaranteed 2-mark derivation question.

def: Work function (phi0) is the minimum energy needed to just remove an electron from the surface of a metal; threshold frequency (v0) is the minimum frequency of light that can cause this emission.
points: Work function depends on the nature of the metal and the condition of its surface.
Metals with low work function (like caesium) show photoelectric effect even with visible light.
Threshold frequency is related to work function by phi0 = h v0.
Below v0, no photoelectrons are emitted no matter how intense the light is.
At exactly v0, electrons are emitted with zero kinetic energy.
Work function is usually expressed in electron-volt (eV) or joule.
formula: phi0 = h v0;  threshold wavelength lambda0 = h c / phi0

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Work function phi0"] --> B["phi0 = h v0"]
  B --> C["Threshold frequency v0"]
  C --> D["v less than v0: no emission"]
  C --> E["v greater than v0: emission occurs"]

example: If phi0 = 4.14 x 10^-19 J and h = 6.63 x 10^-34 Js, then v0 = phi0/h = 6.24 x 10^14 Hz.
tip: Remember the relation phi0 = hv0 connects this topic directly to Einstein's equation — numericals often combine both.

def: Stopping potential (V0) is the minimum negative (retarding) potential applied to the collector plate that just stops the most energetic photoelectrons from reaching it, reducing the photoelectric current to zero.
points: As retarding voltage is increased, photocurrent decreases gradually and becomes zero at V0.
At stopping potential, the work done by the retarding field equals the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons: e V0 = KEmax.
Stopping potential does not depend on the intensity of light, only on its frequency.
A graph of V0 versus frequency v is a straight line with slope h/e.
The intercept of this graph on the frequency axis gives the threshold frequency v0.
This graph experimentally confirms Einstein's photoelectric equation and gives a value of Planck's constant h.
formula: e V0 = h v - phi0, so V0 = (h/e) v - (phi0/e)

diagram.draw: Draw a graph with frequency v on the x-axis and stopping potential V0 on the y-axis. Draw a straight line with positive slope that cuts the x-axis at v0 (threshold frequency) and has slope equal to h/e. Label the line, the slope and the x-intercept v0.

example: If V0 = 1.2 V at frequency 7 x 10^14 Hz, then KEmax = e V0 = 1.2 eV = 1.92 x 10^-19 J.
tip: Draw the V0 vs v graph correctly with the x-intercept labelled v0 — this diagram alone is worth marks in board exams.

def: De Broglie proposed that every moving particle has an associated wave, called a matter wave, whose wavelength depends on its momentum.
points: This dual (particle and wave) nature applies to all matter, not just light.
The de Broglie wavelength is given by lambda = h / p, where p is the momentum of the particle.
For a particle of mass m moving with velocity v, p = mv, so lambda = h / (mv).
Heavier or faster particles have a smaller de Broglie wavelength, so their wave nature is not noticeable in daily life.
For an electron accelerated through potential V, lambda = h / sqrt(2 m e V).
This concept explains the wave-like behaviour observed in electron diffraction experiments.
formula: lambda = h / p = h / (m v) = h / sqrt(2 m e V)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Moving particle mass m velocity v"] --> B["Momentum p = m v"]
  B --> C["De Broglie wavelength lambda = h / p"]
  C --> D["Wave nature observed for very small particles like electrons"]

example: An electron accelerated through 100 V has lambda = h / sqrt(2 m e V) ≈ 1.23 x 10^-10 m, comparable to atomic spacing, so it can diffract through crystals.
tip: Memorise all three forms of the formula (in terms of p, v, and V) since numericals ask for different given quantities.

def: The Davisson-Germer experiment provided the first experimental confirmation of the wave nature of electrons by showing that a beam of electrons diffracts from a nickel crystal just like X-rays.
points: A beam of electrons from an electron gun is accelerated through a known potential and directed onto a nickel crystal.
The scattered electrons are detected at different angles using a movable detector.
A strong peak (maximum intensity) of scattered electrons is observed at a particular angle, similar to diffraction of waves.
This diffraction pattern can only be explained if electrons behave as waves, not just particles.
The wavelength calculated from the diffraction pattern matched closely with the de Broglie wavelength calculated from the electron's momentum.
This experiment confirmed de Broglie's hypothesis of matter waves.
formula: Bragg-like condition used to find wavelength; matches lambda = h / sqrt(2 m e V)

diagram.draw: Draw an electron gun on the left emitting an electron beam towards a nickel crystal target in the centre. Draw a detector mounted on a movable circular scale around the crystal, able to rotate to measure intensity of scattered electrons at angle theta. Label 'electron gun', 'nickel crystal', 'detector', 'angle theta', 'galvanometer'.

example: At accelerating voltage 54 V, a strong diffraction peak was observed at 50 degrees, giving an experimental wavelength that agreed with the de Broglie value of about 1.65 x 10^-10 m.
tip: Mention that the experimental wavelength matching the de Broglie value is the key conclusion — examiners look for this exact statement.
